newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha blames ex-communists for trouble.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha blames ex-communists for trouble.

text.p: President Sali Berisha denounced Albania's former communists on Saturday, saying they were trying to regain power by exploiting five weeks of unrest after a string of popular investment schemes collapsed.
Tens of thousands of people across the Balkan country lost large sums of money after five fraudulent schemes failed last month, sparking a wave of nationwide protests.

"The communists thought it was the right time to swallow Albanian democracy but we will never allow them to take power again," he told some 4,000 boisterous supporters packed into an indoor basketball court.
Berisha was referring to opposition Socialists, who changed their name from the Communist Party after the fall of 45 years of ruthless Stalinist rule in 1990.
"We are sure it was not investors who set fires to public buildings last month but the (former) communists and secret police who want to take power through violence," he said.
It was one of his toughest attacks on the Socialists since anti-government protests erupted last month after the collapse of the investment schemes.
Shkoder, about 35 km (21 miles) from the Yugoslav border, is Albania's main Catholic town and is known for being fiercely anti-communist.

Barisha has criss-crossed the country of 3.4 million to try to regain popular support after being severely criticised by many Albanians for failing to regulate the pyramid schemes and not warning the public of their dangers.
Officials estimate Albanians sank $1 to $2 billion in the fraudulent schemes. Many people earned their money by working illegally at menial jobs overseas.

In the final frenzy, thousands of people also sold homes, property or valuables to pump more money into the pyramids. The schemes counted on money from new investors to pay high interest rates owed to earlier investors.
Berisha was taking no chances in Shkoder. Officials of his ruling Democrats distributed placards to youngsters as they entered the hall, saying "Communism is our Common Ennemy".
The meeting was by invitation only but to ensure the hall was full, Democrat officials handed out fistfuls of invitations to nearby school children who had come to see Barisha.
Police kept a low profile and many of the town's residents seemed unimpressed by their president's visit, going about their routine Saturday chores.
"The meeting is by invitation only, which shows he doesn't trust us," said a man selling rice from a makeshift stand at the dusty central market. "Everything will be well controlled."
Berisha reiterated out his usual list of promises for local development to help counter losses in the pyramids, including making Shkoder an economic free zone.
"We are determined to repair our mistakes," he said.
In Tirana, opposition parties said on Saturday they had been denied permission to stage a mid-day rally in a central soccer stadium, but said the meeting may go ahead anyway.

At the appointed time only the police showed up and no rally took place. Violence flared in the capital on Thursday after a peaceful opposition rally. Scores of protesters clashed with police after the rally ended.
Soccer matches were cancelled for a fifth week because of fears spectators could start anti-government protests.

The free-market government of Berisha and Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi is facing its biggest crisis since coming to power in 1992 and Berisha's campaign to bolster support appears to have had little effect on investors in the country's south.
They have staged daily demonstrations for weeks to demand the government reimburse them for their losses and then resign.
In the Adriatic port town of Vlore, 7,000 marchers turned out for an 18th day and 60 local students started the third day of a hunger strike to demand the government's resignation.
Berisha has said he will travel to Vlore, where three protesters died during street battles with police last week, but no date has been announced for the visit.
